name: Five-plant haemostatic extract (applied to bleeding sites)
short: Applied to wounds: more pain for 2 days in treated molar sockets (50 patients); no major complications in an episiotomy trial. Injected into rat knees: cartilage damage (animal study).
text: This extract is applied directly to bleeding tissue, not taken by mouth; it is named in the cited abstracts by a brand name, and one trial describes it as a standard mixture of Thymus vulgaris, Glycyrrhiza glabra, Vitis vinifera, Alpinia officinarum and Urtica dioica approved in Turkey for bleeding. Harm in people: in a 2014 study of 50 patients who had both lower wisdom teeth removed, the extract was put into one socket and the other was rinsed with saline (physiological serum); dry socket (alveolar osteitis) did not differ significantly between the two sides, but postoperative pain was higher in the treated sockets for the first 2 days. Other trials: in a randomized trial in 40 women having episiotomy repair, in which the extract or saline was applied to the wound on a sponge, no major immediate or delayed complications were seen in either group; in a randomized trial of 90 patients having tubeless kidney-stone surgery (percutaneous nephrolithotomy), complications occurred in 6.6% with the extract and 8.8% without (the abstract gives no statistical test for this); in a randomized trial of 630 patients after transradial catheterisation, haematoma did not differ significantly between the three groups; and in a trial of 50 emergency heart-bypass patients taking clopidogrel and aspirin, in which the extract was sprayed on the heart and surrounding tissue, there were no deaths in either group. In people with hemophilia A, a 2013 study of tooth extractions in 27 patients reports shorter bleeding but gives no adverse-event data in its abstract. In a 2011 single-centre prospective study whose abstract describes no comparison group, the extract was sprayed on bleeding during dental interventions, including after tooth extractions with prolonged bleeding, in 113 patients with normal or impaired blood clotting (the abstract does not say how many had a bleeding disorder); no patient had a wound infection, and healing appeared normal. Animal study: in 21 rats, injecting the extract into the knee, with or without blood, had toxic effects on knee cartilage, and the harm was greater with blood and extract together; the cited sources do not report use inside joints in people. No drug interaction data were found in the cited sources.
